prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test the effect across several distinct problem types, including selective trait learning, broad misbehavior from narrow training, backdoor prevention and hidden transmission.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Item 2
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. A regression model is offered as an illustration and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper present its main claim and its scope?
Option 1: Present the empirical finding as the central contribution and collect its limitations, including model size, LoRA use, and constructed poison data, in a dedicated limitations section.
Option 2: Present the finding as a robust effect shown across trigger paraphrases and several poison types, and describe in the text which negative cases it does and does not rule out.

Item 3
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, treating the match as a check that the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a claim of transfer.
Option 2: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.

Item 4
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.
Option 2: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.

Item 5
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Write a small set of held-out domestic scenarios by hand, run each as a control and a treatment request, and reuse identical wording for every model, seed and sample.
Option 2: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests across varied domains and styles, disjoint from training, and sample each request only a couple of times.

Item 6
Context: A team found a behavior in which a model's final action overrides what its chain of thought concluded. It appears in fine-tuned models and, at a much lower rate, in a few frontier models; a search using value-conflict dilemmas found only one clear case in about one thousand completions. The behavior is rare outside the trained models and its real-world frequency is unestimated. The team must decide what to say about its significance for safety.
Question: How should the team characterize the safety significance of the finding?
Option 1: State that the behavior is concerning for reasoning monitoring even though it is rare, and that a coherent picture of the model's behavior does not emerge by default.
Option 2: Frame the finding as a limit on one monitoring use, noting that models with tool access can give fake justifications in their reasoning so reasoning monitoring needs qualifying.

Item 7
Context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. On a given prompt the models seem to act as one persona or the other. The team wants to measure how often the final answer departs from the plan in the reasoning trace. Rollouts needed thinking-block prefills to yield valid traces. A pre-fine-tuning model and a single-persona model are available for comparison.
Question: How should traces and answers be labeled in the override evaluation?
Option 1: Label traces and answers separately with a language-model judge into pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other, on a few temptation prompts with a single-persona baseline.
Option 2: Label traces and answers with human annotators or a keyword rule check on a small hand-written prompt set, favoring label reliability over the scalability of automated judging.

Item 8
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose a basic-misbehaviour direction based on real deployment data, such as measuring how often current models violate user intent or exploit loopholes on mundane agentic tasks.
Option 2: Propose standalone ideas such as reward hacking that emerges without being rewarded, AI poisoning of training data, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
